title: Shift Coverage: A Step-by-Step Call-Out Playbook
summary: Need shift coverage fast? Follow this six-step call-out playbook to find eligible team members, fill the shift, and confirm it.
body_markdown:
Rhasaan Sherrill, owner and director of[Beat Box Dance Academy](https://www.joinhomebase.com/customers/beat-box-dance-academy-case-study-team-communication) , has a small team and no bench to pull from. “If somebody calls out because they’re sick, I have a small team,” he says. “So finding someone to come in at a drop of a hat and take over the class, that’s always something that kind of gives me anxiety each week.”


That’s the shift coverage problem in one scene. A call-out usually reaches you as a single text, often hours before the shift. What you do next decides whether the shift is covered by 8am or by noon. This guide gives you the sequence to follow: six steps, who’s responsible, a backup plan, and where Homebase fits.


## **How to find shift coverage fast**


The fastest way to cover a last-minute call-out is to confirm it, check who’s eligible, message every eligible team member at once, and approve the first qualified yes. If no one answers, escalate on a clock: split the shift, call your standby list, or cover it yourself.


The six steps at a glance:


1. Confirm the call-out and log it.
2. Check who’s eligible to cover.
3. Send one message to everyone eligible.
4. Approve the cover or swap.
5. Escalate if no one says yes.
6. Confirm the shift and update your schedule.

## **What is shift coverage?**


Shift coverage means having a qualified person working every scheduled position for the whole shift, including a replacement when someone calls out or doesn’t show up. It covers planned gaps, like approved time off, and surprise gaps, like sick calls and no-shows. This guide focuses on the surprise ones.


Three terms come up often, so here’s how they differ:


- **Cover:** One team member picks up another’s shift without trading one back.
- **Shift swap:** Two team members trade scheduled shifts. Our[shift swap guide](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/shift-swap) shows how to set that up.
- **Open shift:** A manager posts a shift with no one assigned, and eligible team members claim it.


## **Who is responsible for finding shift coverage?**


The employee’s job is to give notice through your official call-out channel. The manager’s job is to make sure shift coverage happens. A written policy settles everything in between, like who approves a swap and how much notice you need. Rules vary by state and by employer policy, so check yours.


When no one owns the gap, the owner ends up filling it. Christofer Peralta, a customer success manager in partnerships at Homebase, once visited a restaurant that ran entirely on paper. The schedule on the board was wrong and coverage was off. In his words: “She ended up having to show up mid-shift to cover the floor herself.”


### **Should employees find their own shift coverage?**


It depends on your policy. For a personal request, like a day off, asking the employee to suggest a swap is common. For a sick call, the employee’s job is to tell you. Requiring someone who’s sick to find their own replacement is a policy call to run past HR.


In Homebase, team members can send swap or cover requests to all eligible teammates or to specific people, and you approve each one. Our[shift swapping policies guide](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/shift-swapping-policies) covers how to set the rules.


## **How to find last-minute shift coverage in six steps**


Three things turn a call-out into a scramble: calling people one at a time, having no named owner, and keeping a backup list that’s out of date. Each step below fixes one.


### **Step 1: confirm the call-out and log it**


Take every call-out through one official channel, whether that’s a text, a call, or a message in the app. Log the date, shift, role, how much notice you got, and a reason category. Skip the medical details.


Then name one person who owns shift coverage for that call-out, usually the manager on duty. For more on handling these moments, see our guides on[what to do when an employee calls in sick](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/employee-calling-in-sick-to-work) and[no call no show policies](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/no-call-no-show) .


### **Step 2: check who’s eligible to cover**


Filter before you ask. Eligible means available, not already scheduled, not on approved time off, qualified for the role, and not about to hit overtime or short rest. Federal overtime starts after 40 hours in a workweek for covered nonexempt employees, and some states are stricter, so review your[shift work laws](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/shift-work-laws) .


In Homebase, shift recommendations suggest team members who fit the role, qualifications, availability, and pay rate.


### **Step 3: send one message to everyone eligible**


Message the whole eligible group at once instead of working down a list. A good message states the date, hours, role, and pay, and how to claim the shift. The first qualified yes gets it.


In Homebase, you can[post an open shift](https://www.joinhomebase.com/employee-scheduling/shift-swapping) that shows potential earnings, so eligible team members claim it from the app. They can also get a text inviting them to cover. That’s the end of Sunday-night phone tag.


### **Step 4: approve the cover or swap**


Every cover or swap should go through a manager. Before you say yes, check overtime, qualifications, and pay.


In Homebase, each request comes to you for final approval and shows overtime flags and estimated pay first. Team members can only request swaps with coworkers whose skills, roles, wage rates, and availability are compatible.


### **Step 5: escalate if no one says yes**


Decide the order in advance and give each rung a time limit. Split the shift or stagger start times, call your standby list, then cover it yourself or run short. Set the time limits with your managers so everyone knows when to move to the next rung of your shift coverage plan.


If you end up covering, count the cost. Luanne Ronquillo, owner and founder of Ruru Baked, described what that used to look like: “It would have been like 60-plus hours a week before, because I was doing back of house during the day and then I would do front of house at night if I had to cover a shift.” Gaps that keep reopening are a sign of a bigger problem, and our guide to[understaffing](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/understaffing) can help you spot it.


### **Step 6: confirm the shift and update your schedule**


Confirm with the team member who took it, update your schedule, and tell the team. Then add the call-out to a short log by day and shift, so repeat shift coverage gaps show up.


In Homebase, approved changes update your schedule, updated shifts and pay feed into payroll, and you can view a history of shift changes.

## **Overtime and pay when you cover a shift**


A team member who covers a shift is paid for the hours they work. If those hours push a nonexempt employee past 40 in a workweek, federal law requires overtime pay. That’s at least one and one-half times their regular rate, and some states set stricter rules. A workweek is a fixed 168 hours, and you can’t average hours across weeks, according to the[Department of Labor](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/overtime) and its[Fact Sheet #23](https://www.dol.gov/whd/regs/compliance/whdfs23.htm) .


Say a team member earning $18 an hour is already at 40 hours and covers a six-hour shift. At overtime, that shift costs $162 (18 × 1.5 × 6). At straight time, it would cost $108.


That $54 difference is why you check eligibility before you ask. For more on how overtime works, see our guide to[overtime and double time pay](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/calculating-double-time-pay) .


## **Build a backup plan before the next call-out**


Shift coverage works best when your backup list and availability are current before anyone calls out. Tracking team availability is part of Advanced Scheduling, which comes with the Essentials plan and up.


### **Keep a standby list**


Ask team members who want short-notice shifts to opt in, and tag them by role. Review the list monthly and drop anyone who keeps declining. Rotate offers so the same few people don’t take every extra shift, which keeps shift coverage fair.


### **Cross-train your team**


Team members who can work more than one role give you more options when someone calls out. Even a few hours of training on a second station widens your shift coverage options.


## **How to write a call-out and shift swap policy**


A short written shift coverage policy keeps call-outs from turning into arguments. Cover these points:


- **Call-out channel:** Name one official way to report a call-out.
- **Notice:** Set a minimum notice for swaps. We recommend 24 to 48 hours as a baseline.
- **Approval:** Say who approves swaps and covers.
- **Even trades:** Spell out the rules for hours, pay, skill, and role.
- **Overtime:** Explain how you handle swaps that push someone past 40 hours.
- **Repeat no-shows:** State what repeated no-shows lead to.


Fair workweek and predictive scheduling laws vary by city and state, so check local rules before you finalize. ## **Frequently asked questions about shift coverage**


### **What is shift coverage?**


Shift coverage means having a qualified person working every scheduled position for the whole shift, including replacements when someone calls out or doesn’t show up. It covers planned gaps, like time off, and surprise gaps, like sick calls. A cover, a swap, and an open shift are three ways to fill the gap.


### **Do I still get paid if someone covers my shift?**


Usually not for the hours you don’t work. If a coworker covers your shift, you aren’t working it, so wages aren’t owed unless paid leave applies, such as PTO or paid sick leave under your employer’s policy or state law. The coworker is paid for the hours they work. Check your handbook and local rules.


### **Can an employer force you to cover a shift?**


Often, yes. Federal law doesn’t limit how many hours employees 16 and older can be scheduled to work, but overtime pay applies after 40 hours in a workweek. State or city rules, union contracts, and employer policy may add limits, so check local rules before requiring anyone to cover.


### **Are you required to find coverage for a shift?**


That depends on your employer’s policy, not a single federal rule. Many employers ask employees to give notice and leave finding cover to the manager, especially for sick calls. Others let employees suggest a swap for personal requests. Check your handbook, and managers should write the rule into a policy.


### **When you cover someone’s shift, do you get paid?**


Yes. An employee who covers a shift is paid for the hours they work. If those hours push a covered nonexempt employee past 40 in a workweek, federal law requires overtime of at least one and one-half times the regular rate, and some states set stricter rules.


### **How do you find last-minute shift coverage?**


Confirm the call-out, check who’s eligible, and message all of them at once instead of calling one by one. Approve the first qualified yes. If no one answers within your time limit, split the shift, call your standby list, or cover it yourself. Then update your schedule and log the call-out.


### **How can team messaging improve shift coverage?**


One message reaches every eligible employee at the same moment, so you aren’t working down a list one person at a time. A good message states the date, hours, role, and pay, and the first qualified reply gets the shift. In Homebase, open shifts can show potential earnings so eligible employees can claim them in the app.


## **Make call-outs a routine, not an emergency**


Call-outs will keep happening, especially in cold and flu season. What changes is whether you scramble or follow a shift coverage plan. Check who’s eligible before you ask, write down your policy, and keep your standby list current.
